title: Before you draw
say: Welcome! Let’s get ready to draw together. We’ll gather your tools, make a comfortable space, and try a few pencil marks. You don’t need experience. After each little step, I’ll wait for you. Press Continue when you’re ready.

title: Your pencil toolkit
say: Find your pencils: 2H, HB, 2B, 3B, 4B and 6B. The harder pencils help with light construction lines. The softer ones build richer darks. Lay them out where you can see the labels. Take your time. I’ll wait here.

title: Blending and erasing
say: You’ll also need a blending stump or tissue to soften your shading. A kneaded eraser lifts graphite gently, and a regular eraser helps with sharper corrections. Find those now. An easel and artist tape are optional; a comfortable desk works too.
hint: Blending tool · Kneaded eraser · Regular eraser

title: Feel your sketch paper
say: Here is real sketch paper. Look closely at these two paper samples. The more textured surface has tiny bumps that catch the graphite. The smoother sample has a finer grain. Now gently feel both sides of your own sheet. Either side can work. For this lesson, choose the rougher side, so the paper texture shows through your pencil marks. Tap a photo for a closer look, then put your chosen side facing up.
hint: Look closely. Feel your own paper.

title: Choose your paper size
say: A4 is a handy starting size: twenty-one by twenty-nine point seven centimetres. Letter size works too, and you can choose another size you enjoy. Keep a spare piece nearby for practice marks. Put your chosen drawing side facing up.

title: Your kit is ready
say: You’ve gathered what you need. That’s a real first step! Having your tools nearby gives you more room to enjoy drawing. Now let’s make a little space for you.

title: Make room to draw
say: Now arrange your own space. Keep the paper in front of you, and your tools within easy reach. An angled surface can help, but a desk is fine. I’ll wait while you make yourself comfortable.

title: Keep your paper still
say: If your paper slips, use gentle artist tape at the edges. Four edges are plenty for our cube practice. The teacher’s fuller taping is useful when drawing a background. This step is optional. If your paper stays still, you’re ready to move on.

title: Relax your shoulders
say: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Keep room for your arm to move. Big strokes can come from your shoulder, while small details use your fingers. Take one easy breath. There’s no need to rush.

title: Room to create
say: Your space is ready, and you’ve given yourself room to move. Nice work taking care of the little things. Now let’s get to know your pencil.

title: A loose, sweeping grip
say: Look at the hand in this picture. Holding farther from the pencil tip gives your arm room for wider, lighter strokes. Try that grip and make a few loose lines on your spare paper. You don’t need to make them perfect.
hint: Farther from the tip → freer movement

title: Find your comfortable grip
say: These left and right-handed examples both work. Holding closer to the tip gives more control for small details. Try moving your grip closer, then farther away. Keep your fingers soft. Choose what feels comfortable for the marks you’re making.

title: Loose
say: Try a small patch of spaced lines. I’ll wait. Continue when you’re ready.
watchSay: We’re starting with loose hatching. Watch the teacher leave little gaps between these upright lines. Light pressure, steady direction.

title: Dense
say: Try a denser patch beside it. Compare the gaps. Take your time.
watchSay: Now watch dense hatching. The upright lines sit closer together, covering more paper. More lines, rather than a hard squeeze, make the patch fuller.

title: Horizontal
say: Your turn: a few horizontal rows. Keep your hand relaxed.
watchSay: This time the strokes travel sideways. Watch the teacher repeat horizontal lines, keeping their direction steady.

title: Diagonal
say: Try a patch of diagonal strokes. It’s fine if they wobble.
watchSay: Now the lines lean diagonally. Follow that slant with your eyes. Each stroke travels in the same direction.

title: Point Tip
say: Try drawing with the point. Notice how narrow each mark feels.
watchSay: Watch the pencil tip. The pointed tip makes clear, narrow diagonal marks. A relaxed grip helps you place them.

title: Side of Lead
say: Try the side of the lead. Compare its softer marks with your pointed strokes.
watchSay: Now watch the side of the lead touch the paper. It makes broader, softer marks than the point. Compare the texture on your right.

title: Staggered
say: Let your stroke ends overlap at different places. Try a small patch.
watchSay: Here the teacher staggers the strokes. Their ends overlap at different places, so they don’t all stop on one hard line.

title: Dark to Light
say: Try moving from dark to light across your patch. Aim for a gentle change.
watchSay: Watch the patch move from dark on the left to light on the right. The teacher gradually eases the pressure.

title: Top Dark, Bottom Light
say: Try dark at the top and light below. I’ll wait while you explore it.
watchSay: Now the dark area is at the top. Watch the horizontal strokes become lighter as the teacher moves down.

title: Diagonal Gradient
say: Try a diagonal change in tone. Your patch doesn’t have to match perfectly.
watchSay: This gradient follows a diagonal direction. Notice how lighter and darker strokes change the tone across the patch.

title: Dark Edges, Light Center
say: Try two darker edges with a light center. Ease up gradually.
watchSay: Watch both edges become darker while the middle stays lighter. Let the pressure ease toward that light center.

title: Light Edges, Dark Center
say: Try a darker center with lighter edges. Keep the transitions soft.
watchSay: Now reverse it: light edges, dark center. The teacher builds the strongest tone in the middle and softens it toward the sides.

title: Single Layer
say: Try one even layer of lines. Notice the paper still showing between them.
watchSay: Here comes one layer of upright strokes. Watch the spacing and direction. This is the foundation for building more tone.

title: Double Layer
say: Add another direction over your first layer. Notice what changes.
watchSay: Now the teacher adds a second direction over the first layer. Where the strokes cross, the patch becomes richer.

title: Multi-Layer
say: Try building several gentle layers. You’ve explored all fifteen patterns. Continue when you’re ready.
watchSay: Watch several light layers build this final patch. Changing direction fills more gaps. Build gradually instead of pressing hard.

title: You showed up and practised
say: You tried the marks, and that’s what matters. Your page doesn’t need to look like the teacher’s yet. Every thoughtful attempt helps you notice more. Let’s carry that curiosity into the next step.

title: Notice near and far
say: Here’s one idea to take into the cube lesson: things farther away look smaller. Look at the near and far parts of this reference. Point to one part that seems closer to you.

title: Follow the receding lines
say: Look at the lines that travel away from you. They appear to come closer together in the distance. You can spot this in a hallway or along a road too. That’s enough for now; we’ll use this idea when drawing the cube.

title: Wake up your hand
say: Open and close your hand ten times, gently. Wiggle your fingers and slowly roll your wrist both ways. Then make ten loose squiggles on scrap paper. Stay comfortable; stop any movement that hurts. I’ll wait until you’re ready.

title: Ready to draw
say: Look at everything you’ve done: your tools are ready, your space is comfortable, and you’ve tried your first marks. Well done taking it one step at a time. You’re ready to bring those ideas into the cube. I’ll see you there.
